summary:
Michoacán has not typified the killing of LGBT people as a hate crime under state law, an absence acknowledged by the state's own welfare officials and by civil-society monitors. Attacks against the community concentrate geographically in Tierra Caliente, the zone of armed-group influence, so risk inside the state is uneven rather than uniform: Morelia, the state capital, records the largest absolute number of LGBT homicides, but enforcement of any protective framework is weak throughout.

Homicide against LGBT people in Michoacán is sustained and documented. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes contra Personas LGBT, presented by Raúl Martínez of Colectivo Michoacán es Diversidad, counted 46 LGBT homicides in the state between 2015 and 2024, distributed across Morelia (11), Lázaro Cárdenas (6), Apatzingán and Uruapan (5 each) and Zamora (4). The deadliest year was 2015, with 10 victims. Trans women accounted for 27 of the 46 homicides, and the 25 to 39 age bracket was the most affected. Thirteen disappearances of LGBT people were reported between 2022 and 2024, a figure whose investigation status the civil-society data does not resolve.

The pattern continued into 2026. Six homicide cases against LGBT people were identified in the state in the first four and a half months of that year, three in Morelia and one each in Uruapan, Ocampo and Maravatío. One of them was 'Daniela', a trans woman found beaten to death in a drainage channel in Morelia on 2 April 2026; a suspect was arrested, an outcome that stands out against the surrounding pattern of inaction. At least 56 aggressions against the community have been registered in Michoacán since 2014.

Impunity is the decisive variable for a visitor assessing protection. Of the 46 hate-crime cases recorded by civil society in the state since 2015, only one was moving toward judicial proceedings: the murder of Meredith Escarlet, a trans woman killed in Tarímbaro. The state prosecutor's office keeps no disaggregated data on these cases, and the victims commission, the state human rights commission and the state council against discrimination lack the capacity or budget to act. No public prevention policy for LGBT violence exists in the state.
